Selected work

Co-op work is described without internal part numbers, document numbers or customer names. Hardware images and diagrams have been withheld to protect Vicor Corporation’s IP. Happy to go deeper in conversation.

01

Finding out why plating was shorting capacitor terminals

Root cause analysis · Vicor Corporation

Overview

Assemblies were coming off the line with plating bridged across the terminals of some capacitors. The CAD assembly said there was clearance between the mold compound and the board. The parts said there wasn’t. I was asked to work out which of the two was wrong.

What I did

  • Sectioned finished assemblies and measured the mold-compound-to-PCB distance optically on both faces of the board.
  • Took the same measurement out of the CAD assembly at nominal and at maximum material condition, so the model and the hardware could be compared on identical terms.
  • Compared them face by face and found the parts fell outside the modeled envelope in both directions — about 267 µm tighter than the model on one face, and roughly 117 µm wider than nominal on the other.
  • Wrote the comparison up with the section images alongside the model dimensions, so the result could be read without re-running the analysis.

Outcome

The model did not bound the manufactured condition on either face. The clearance the design was relying on to keep plating away from the capacitor terminals was not present on real parts — which moved the conversation from tightening the process to correcting the drawing.

Tools & methods

SolidWorksOptical measurementGD&TMaximum material conditionRoot cause analysis
02

A liquid-cooled fixture for testing four power modules at once

Fixture design · Vicor Corporation

Overview

Testing a 2×2 array of power modules means holding three things steady at the same time: the electrical contact, the clamping load, and the heat path — while still letting an operator swap parts in and out quickly. I detailed the mechanical hardware for the revised platform and took it through design review.

What I did

  • Detailed the spring-loaded plunger assembly that carries clamping load onto the array — sleeve, foot, carbide wear plate and retainer — as a released drawing set.
  • Specified 6061-T6 aluminum throughout, black anodize to MIL-A-8625F Type II Class 2, RoHS compliant, with burr-free and residue-free supply called out on every part.
  • Designed the pogo-pin contact blocks that make the electrical connection without soldering, so modules can be loaded and removed repeatedly without rework.
  • Presented the revised platform at design review, including the temperature drop across the thermal interface.

Outcome

A repeatable water-cooled test setup for a four-module array, with the contact and clamping hardware defined well enough to be built from the drawings alone.

Tools & methods

SolidWorksGD&TDesign reviewDFMAnodized aluminumPogo-pin contacts
03

Low-profile liquid cooling for a converter evaluation platform

Thermal hardware · Vicor Corporation

Overview

An evaluation platform for a high-current converter needed cooling on both faces, in a height budget too tight for the coil-spring clamp stack normally used. The concept was a matched pair of heat exchangers closing on the module from above and below. I turned that concept into manufacturable hardware.

What I did

  • Detailed the upper and lower heat exchanger bodies, the lower cover, and the elastomer face seal that closes the coolant cavity.
  • Worked to a Belleville washer clamp rather than coil springs — a roughly 6 mm spring footprint against the 9–12 mm a coil spring would need, which is where the height came from.
  • Kept the pre-assembly thermal faces flat and unobstructed so interface material can be stenciled straight onto the heat exchangers, with the mounting screws installed blind afterwards.
  • Carried a load-spreading plate through the drawings so the small washer footprint doesn’t translate into uneven pressure across the module.

Outcome

A sealed, complementary heat exchanger pair, drawn for manufacture, that cools the converter from both faces inside the platform’s height limit.

Tools & methods

SolidWorksThermal interface materialsBelleville spring loadingSeal designDetail drafting
04

Air cooling an array that a fan on a heatsink can’t handle

Thermal hardware · Vicor Corporation

Overview

The brief was to air cool a three-up module array shedding up to around 100 W per side, where derating starts somewhere near 60–70 °C. A heatsink with an axial fan bolted to it doesn’t get the thermal resistance low enough, and ducting the air to where the fins actually are costs 0.5–1.5 inches of water in back pressure. That makes it a blower problem rather than a fan problem, and it has to be sealed. I did the mechanical design for the cooling system.

What I did

  • Designed the ducting that splits flow three ways across the array, and the transition from the blower outlet into the plenum inlet.
  • Packaged the ducting and modules as a cartridge that plugs into an air socket, so a module set can be swapped without rebuilding the plenum around it.
  • Designed the heatsinks for the array, working to a module pitch roughly 3:2 wider than the liquid-cooled version to leave room for the fin stacks and the air to move between them.
  • Drew the plenum kit, cartridge and duct assemblies for manufacture.
  • Reworked the copper heatsink design into 3D printable facsimiles so the whole assembly could be built and reviewed before committing time and money to machined copper.

Outcome

A sealed, ducted cooling system for a three-up array, carried to a 3D printed mock-up that could be handled and reviewed before any money went into machined copper.
